title: Early years, the life course and health
blurb: Explain how early childhood and adversity shape later health, and apply a life course approach from conception to older age.
question: Shane, 31, attends the emergency department for the fourth time this year after an assault while drunk. He mentions that he grew up with a father in prison and a mother who drank heavily. How might his childhood relate to his health now, and what approach should the nurse take?

teach.body: A life course approach to health considers the critical stages, transitions and settings where large differences can be made in promoting or restoring health and wellbeing, rather than focusing on one disease at one age. In plain English: what happens before birth and in childhood carries forward, risks build up over a lifetime, and every stage offers a chance to help. Public Health England's life course stages run from preconception through early years, childhood and adolescence, and working age to older people.
teach.cite: PHE, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (23 May 2019)

teach.caption: Marmot Review: the earliest years of life set the tone for the whole lifespan.

teach.body: ACEs are stressful experiences in childhood, including abuse and household stressors. The Welsh ACE study (Public Health Wales and Liverpool John Moores University, 2015) surveyed about 2,000 adults about nine ACEs. 47% had experienced at least one and 14% had four or more. Compared with people with no ACEs, those with four or more were far more likely to have health-harming behaviours as adults.
teach.cite: Bellis et al., Welsh ACE study (2015)

teach.caption: Household items refer to what happened to adults in the child's home, for example a parent in prison or domestic violence between adults.

teach.h: 4+ ACEs vs none: how many times more likely
teach.caption: Welsh ACE study (2015). Teenage pregnancy was also about 6 times more likely.

teach.body: PHE describes maintaining good functional ability as the main outcome of the life course approach. Functional ability combines intrinsic capacity (a person's physical and mental abilities) with their environment, such as glasses, dropped kerbs, safe streets and suitable housing. When intrinsic capacity is still developing (children) or reduced (illness, disability, ageing), the environment matters even more. Depression affects around 22% of men and 28% of women aged 65 and over, yet most do not receive help.
teach.cite: PHE, Health matters: life course approach (2019)

teach.h: Scenario: Shane in the emergency department
teach.body: Staff nurse Ola treats Shane's injuries and notes his history: a parent in prison, a parent misusing alcohol and, he adds, violence at home. That is at least three ACEs. Ola knows ACEs are linked with heavy drinking and being a victim of violence, so she avoids judgement and asks what support he would accept. With his agreement she refers him to the hospital alcohol liaison team. She also asks whether there are children at home, since ACEs can pass between generations.

teach.text: ACEs raise the LIKELIHOOD of harm; they do not decide anyone's future. Most people with ACEs do not go on to these outcomes, and support at any stage helps. Also, household ACEs count even if the child was never harmed directly: witnessing domestic violence is an ACE.

items: Life course approach: critical stages, transitions and settings; preconception to older age.
First 1,000 days (pregnancy to age 2) can make a difference over a whole lifetime.
Welsh ACE study: nine ACEs; 47% at least one; 14% four or more.
4+ ACEs vs none: 4× high-risk drinking, 6× smoking, 14× violence victim, 20× incarceration.
Adolescence: brain changes more than at any time apart from the first 3 years.
Main outcome: functional ability = intrinsic capacity + supportive environment.

summary: You can now explain how early years and adverse childhood experiences influence later health and behaviour, using the Welsh ACE study. You can also apply a life course approach across stages from preconception to older age, focused on functional ability.

A.q: The 2015 Welsh study asked adults about a defined set of adverse childhood experiences. How many types of ACE did it include?
A.why: The Welsh ACE study measured nine ACEs covering childhood abuse and household stressors.

whyNot.0: Five is too few; the study included three types of abuse and six household stressors.
whyNot.1: Seven is not the number measured.
whyNot.3: Twelve is more than the study measured.

A.q: Which period does PHE describe as able to make a difference across a child's whole lifetime?
A.why: PHE (2019): the first 1,000 days of a child's life (from conception to age 2) can make a difference over their whole lifetime.

whyNot.0: 100 days is far shorter than the period described.
whyNot.1: School years matter, but the period highlighted is the first 1,000 days.
whyNot.3: Adolescence is a critical period, but the period highlighted as shaping the whole lifetime is the first 1,000 days.

A.q: A school nurse is explaining ACEs. Which of these is one of the nine ACEs in the Welsh study?
options: Being the youngest of several siblings
Attending more than one primary school
Growing up with a parent in prison
A.why: Incarceration of a household member is one of the nine ACEs, alongside abuse, parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse and drug use.

whyNot.0: House moves may be stressful but are not one of the nine ACEs measured.
whyNot.1: Birth order is not an ACE.
whyNot.2: Changing school is not one of the nine ACEs.

B.q: A practice nurse reads that Welsh adults reporting four or more ACEs were far more likely than those with none to have spent time in prison. Approximately how many times more likely?
B.why: Welsh ACE study (2015): adults with 4+ ACEs were about 20 times more likely to have been incarcerated.

whyNot.0: About 4 times is the figure for high-risk drinking.
whyNot.1: About 6 times is the figure for smoking.
whyNot.2: About 11 times is the figure for cannabis use.

B.q: Mr Fairbairn, 84, has lived alone since his wife died and is determined to stay in his bungalow. Under PHE's life course approach, which outcome should his care plan mainly aim to maintain?
B.why: PHE (2019): maintaining good functional ability is the main outcome of the life course approach; it combines intrinsic capacity and a supportive environment.

whyNot.1: BMI is a single risk measure, not the main life course outcome.
whyNot.2: BP control matters for some people but is a disease-specific target.
whyNot.3: Service use is not the outcome measure.

B.q: Kayden, 6, often hears his father shouting at and hitting his mother at night. Kayden has never been physically hurt himself. Which statement is accurate?
options: Kayden has no ACEs because he has not been harmed
Witnessing domestic violence counts as an ACE
ACEs count when abuse is reported to police
B.why: Domestic violence in the household is one of the nine ACEs, whether or not the child is hurt directly. Safeguarding procedures also apply.

whyNot.0: Household ACEs include exposure to domestic violence between adults.
whyNot.1: There is no age threshold of 12; ACEs cover all of childhood.
whyNot.3: ACEs are experiences, whether or not they were reported.

C.q: A community nursing team lead wants the new borough health plan to follow PHE's life course approach. Which principle should shape it?
options: Focus resources on older adults, as they use most services
Treat each disease separately at the age when it appears
Concentrate on early years and stop at school age
Act at critical stages and transitions across life
C.why: PHE: a life course approach considers critical stages, transitions and settings across the whole of life, unlike a disease-oriented approach focused on one condition at one stage.

whyNot.0: Focusing on one age group ignores earlier opportunities.
whyNot.1: A disease-by-disease approach is what the life course approach contrasts with.
whyNot.2: Early years matter most, but action is needed at every stage, including working and older age.

C.q: Tyler, 15, is admitted after drinking heavily at a party. His mother asks why the team are offering so much support at his age. Which explanation is consistent with PHE's life course approach?
options: The teenage brain changes more than at any time since age 3
Adolescents rarely change behaviour, so intervention must be intensive
Health habits are fixed by 12, so this is mainly damage limitation
Teenagers are legally adults for health decisions at 15
C.why: PHE (2019): adolescence is a critical period and window of opportunity; brains develop and change more during the teenage years than at any other time apart from the first 3 years of life.

whyNot.1: Adolescence is described as a window of opportunity, not a time when change is unlikely.
whyNot.2: Habits are not fixed by 12; adolescence offers real opportunity.
whyNot.3: At 15 he is not legally an adult; consent rules for under-16s differ.

C.q: Using the Welsh ACE study, what proportion of adults reported four or more ACEs?
C.why: Welsh ACE study (2015): 14% of adults reported four or more ACEs; 47% reported at least one.

whyNot.2: 47% is the proportion with at least one ACE.

reteach.title: Risks add up, chances come round
reteach.question: Why does a nurse caring for an adult need to think about that person's childhood, and their children?

blocks.body: Risks accumulate: a hard start in life, without support, makes harmful coping (drinking, smoking, drugs) and illness more likely later. But each stage offers a new chance: pregnancy, the early years, adolescence, a hospital admission in adulthood, retirement. Asking about the past, without judgement, explains the present; asking about the children at home protects the next generation.

blocks.text: 47% is 'at least one ACE'; 14% is 'four or more'. Keep the two numbers apart.

explain.body: Critical stages, transitions and settings from preconception through early years, childhood and adolescence, working age and older age. Contrasts with a disease-by-disease approach.

test.q: Which is a life stage in PHE's life course approach?
test.why: PHE's stages: preconception; early years; childhood and adolescence; working age; older people.

whyNot.1: Retirement is a transition within the life course, not one of the named stages.
whyNot.3: An admission is a setting or event, not a stage.

explain.body: Nine ACEs: verbal, physical and sexual abuse; parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse, drug use and incarceration in the household. 47% at least one; 14% four or more.

test.q: Which household experience is one of the nine ACEs?
test.why: Parental separation is one of the household ACEs in the Welsh study.

whyNot.0: Housing type is not an ACE.
whyNot.2: Family composition alone is not an ACE.
whyNot.3: Moving home is not one of the nine.

explain.body: 4+ ACEs vs none: about 4× high-risk drinking, 6× smoking, 6× teenage pregnancy, 11× cannabis, 14× violence victim, 15× perpetrator, 16× crack or heroin, 20× incarceration.

test.q: In the Welsh ACE study, adults with four or more ACEs were about how many times more likely to be high-risk drinkers than those with none?
test.why: Welsh ACE study (2015): about 4 times more likely to be high-risk drinkers.

whyNot.2: 11 times is the figure for cannabis use.
whyNot.3: 16 times is the figure for crack cocaine or heroin use.

explain.body: Functional ability = intrinsic capacity + environment. Supportive environments (housing, transport, aids) matter most when capacity is reduced. Depression affects about 22% of men and 28% of women over 65; most do not get help.

items: Look for depression in older people

test.q: Arthur, 79, has poor eyesight and has stopped going out. Which change best improves his functional ability, as PHE describes it?
options: Advising him to stay in to avoid falls
Increasing home visits so he need not go out
Arranging an eye test and suitable glasses
test.why: PHE: functional ability can be boosted by supportive factors, giving glasses to correct poor vision as an example, so he can do what he values.

whyNot.0: Staying in reduces activity and social contact.
whyNot.1: More visits may help but do not restore his ability to go out.
whyNot.3: Monitoring BMI does not address the barrier.
